cues.text: The Empty Tomb
Early on the first day of the week, women came to anoint the crucified body of Jesus.
They found the stone rolled away from His tomb outside the walls of Jerusalem, and the tomb itself empty.
All four Gospels agree on this central fact, even as they differ in the small details naturally found among independent eyewitness accounts.
An angel announced to the women that Christ was risen, just as He had foretold.

The empty tomb alone did not create faith in the Resurrection; it was the personal appearances of the risen Lord that transformed frightened, scattered disciples into fearless witnesses willing to die for what they had seen.
Appearances of the Risen Christ
Over the following weeks, the risen Christ appeared repeatedly.
He appeared to Mary Magdalene weeping at the tomb, to two disciples on the road to Emmaus, and to Peter.
He appeared to the assembled disciples in the upper room, first without Thomas and then, a week later, with Thomas present so that he could touch Christ's wounds.
He appeared to seven disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and, as St. Paul records, to more than five hundred brethren at once — most of whom were still living when Paul wrote of it.
These appearances were physical and repeated, not visionary or symbolic.
The risen Christ ate broiled fish.
He invited Thomas to touch His hands and side.
He walked and spoke with His followers over an extended period.
Theological Significance of the Resurrection
For the Church, the Resurrection is not one miracle among many but the foundation of the entire Gospel.
St. Paul stated plainly that if Christ has not been raised, Christian faith is empty and preaching is in vain.
The Resurrection vindicates Christ's own claims to divinity, seals His victory over sin and death, and guarantees the future bodily resurrection of all believers.
It is likewise the reason the early Church shifted its principal day of worship from the Jewish Sabbath to Sunday , the 'first day of the week,' commemorating the day of the Resurrection.
The Ascension into Heaven
According to the Acts of the Apostles, Christ appeared to His disciples over forty days, instructing them about the Kingdom of God.
He then led them out toward Bethany , near the Mount of Olives.
There, in their sight, He was lifted up and a cloud took Him from their view.
Two men in white robes told the astonished Apostles that this same Jesus would return one day in like manner.
The Ascension is not a departure into absence.
It is Christ's exaltation to 'the right hand of the Father,' where, in the Church's ancient confession, He reigns as Lord and continually intercedes for His people.
From Ascension to Pentecost: The Waiting Church
Before ascending, Christ commanded the Apostles not to leave Jerusalem but to await 'the promise of the Father' — the coming of the Holy Spirit.
The Eleven, together with Mary the Mother of Jesus and other disciples, returned to the city and devoted themselves to prayer in the upper room.
This ten-day interval between Ascension and Pentecost has traditionally shaped the Church's own novena of prayer awaiting the Holy Spirit.
It also marks the transition from Christ's earthly ministry to the visible birth of the Church at Pentecost.
Legacy: The Cornerstone of Christian Faith
Every subsequent article of Christian belief and every century covered by this timeline rests on the conviction that these two events truly happened in history.
Councils, martyrdoms, missions, and devotions across two thousand years all presuppose an empty tomb in Jerusalem and an ascended Lord who, the Church holds, will come again.
The Resurrection and Ascension are commemorated liturgically every year — at Easter, and on Ascension Thursday, the fortieth day of Eastertide.
They are proclaimed at every Mass in the words 'Christ has died, Christ is risen, Christ will come again.'
